verses.note: The Spirit's first appearance in Scripture is at creation, present and active over what is not yet ordered. The Old Testament later speaks of the Spirit giving life (Psalm 104:30), a thread the New Testament picks up when it speaks of the Spirit's work of new creation.

The breath God gave in 2:7 is his to give and to withdraw. Human life depends moment by moment on God's Spirit (Psalm 104:29-30, Job 34:14-15), and this verse is the first time God says he will limit it.

In the Old Testament the Spirit of God gives wisdom, skill, and capacity to lead, not only prophecy. Pharaoh likely meant something within his own religion, but the narrator lets his words point to the true source of Joseph's gifts, as Nebuchadnezzar's words about Daniel will later do (Daniel 4:8).

The Messiah is the Spirit-bearer. The Gospels show the Spirit descending and remaining on Jesus at his baptism (John 1:32-33), and in Nazareth Jesus reads the related promise of Isaiah 61:1 as fulfilled in himself. Christian theology has drawn from this verse that the Son's human life was lived in dependence on the Spirit.

Jeremiah does not name the Spirit, but Ezekiel's parallel promise joins the new heart to God's Spirit within (Ezekiel 36:26-27), and Paul reads the two together when he calls the Corinthians a letter written ‘with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts’ (2 Corinthians 3:3).

The Old Testament knew the Spirit coming on judges, prophets, and kings for particular tasks. Here the Spirit is promised to the whole people, permanently, within, and for ordinary obedience. That promise is what Joel 2:28-29 announces and what Peter declares fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-18, 33).

The Spirit who will give life to the bones in verse 14 is first the Spirit who brings the prophet into the valley. The chapter begins and ends with God's Spirit acting: carrying the messenger, then raising the dead.

The Spirit is here the giver of life, the role the Nicene Creed confesses when it names the Holy Spirit as Lord and giver of life. Ezekiel ties the Spirit to both the new heart (36:26-27) and the raising of the dead, the two works Paul joins when he says the Spirit who raised Jesus will give life to believers' mortal bodies (Romans 8:11).

The grief that leads to cleansing (13:1) does not begin with the people; it begins when God pours out his Spirit. Repentance is presented as God's gift before it is the people's act, the pattern of Acts 2, where Peter's hearers are cut to the heart after the Spirit is poured out.

The prophets promised that God would pour out his Spirit on his people (Joel 2:28-29, Ezekiel 36:25-27). John says the coming one will do this, which assigns to Jesus a work the Old Testament reserves for God.
The Spirit comes upon Jesus to equip him as the anointed one, in line with Isaiah 42:1 and 61:1. The one who will baptize with the Spirit first receives the Spirit.
The Spirit who came upon Jesus at his baptism (1:10) will speak through his followers on trial. Acts shows it happening with Peter before the council (Acts 4:8).

The witnesses are not sent in their own strength. The Spirit is the Father's promise, sent by the risen Son, and given as power for witness; the Trinitarian shape of the church's mission is already present in the Gospel's last words.

The Spirit rests on Jesus so that Jesus can give the Spirit to others. The Gospel keeps that promise when the risen Jesus breathes on the disciples and says ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (20:22); Acts 2 tells of the outpouring at Pentecost.
The Spirit is the agent of the new birth. Whatever the water means, the whole sentence makes the Spirit the one who gives entrance to the kingdom.

The Spirit is free. He cannot be commanded, predicted, or institutionally controlled, and yet his work is real and audible. The verse guards against making new birth either a human technique or an invisible idea without effects.

The Spirit rests on Jesus without limit, fulfilling the Baptist's sign that the Spirit would remain on him (1:32-33). Because the Spirit is his without measure, he can give the Spirit to others (7:39, 20:22).

Wind and fire are Old Testament signs of God's presence (Exodus 3:2, 19:18; Ezekiel 37:9). Their coming on each person, not on the group as a whole or on the apostles alone, says that the Spirit now rests on every member of the community, as he rested on Jesus at his baptism.
The Spirit is the giver of the speech. The disciples do not produce the gift and then ascribe it to God; Luke says the Spirit kept giving them the words.

In the Old Testament the Spirit came on particular people: prophets, judges, kings, craftsmen. Joel promised a day when the Spirit would come on all God's people without distinction of sex, age, or status, and Peter says that day has come.
The Spirit's coming is the exalted Christ's gift. The Spirit does not replace Jesus but comes from him and testifies to his reign.
